title: Whether SARFAESI Act Overrides MPID Act In Recovery Of Dues? Supreme Court Refers To Larger Bench
case_name: National Spot Exchange Ltd. v. Union of India
ratio: The overriding provisions of the MPID Act and the SARFAESI Act must be harmoniously reconciled to ensure their effective operation.
summary: The Supreme Court on Thursday (November 26) referred to a larger bench the dispute over the priority of claims under the Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002 (SARFAESI Act) and the Maharashtra Protection of Interest of Depositors (in Financial Establishments) Act, 1999 (MPID Act), after expressing disagreement with a coordinate bench ruling in National Spot Exchange Ltd. v. Union of India (NSEL) which had accorded priority to claims under the MPID Act over those under the Centrally enacted Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC).

note.Facts: SBI extended credit to a borrower who mortgaged property; the loan became NPA and SBI invoked SARFAESI-Act security. The borrower was later found to have duped depositors under the MPID Act. Maharashtra seized the same properties, directed SBI to obtain permission under the MPID Act, and later attached the properties, allocating sale proceeds to depositors. SBI sought to appropriate the surplus towards its secured debt; lower courts rejected the claim, relying on *NSEL*.
note.Issue: Whether, in a conflict between the SARFAESI Act, 2002 and the Maharashtra Protection of Interest of Depositors (MPID) Act, 1999, the SARFAESI Act gives priority to secured creditors over the claims of depositors protected under the MPID Act.
note.Held: The two-Judge bench declined to decide the matter and referred the questions of priority and dominant legislation to a larger bench, expressing the view that the SARFAESI Act, being a later central enactment, is likely to prevail over the MPID Act.
note.Principle: When a central law (SARFAESI Act) and a state law (MPID Act) overlap on the recovery of dues, the doctrine of “dominant legislation” requires harmonious construction, giving priority to secured creditors under the SARFAESI Act unless the state law expressly provides a contrary priority; the later-enacted, non-obstante clause and the inclusion of Section 26E strengthen the SARFAESI Act’s priority.
note.Provisions: SARFAESI Act – Section 35 (non-obstante clause), Section 26E; MPID Act – Section 14 (non-obstante clause), Section 26E (comparative reference); *National Spot Exchange Ltd. v. Union of India* (NSEL) (precedent questioned). No other statutes or cases cited.
note.Exam angle: Test on the SARFAESI Act – priority of secured debt vs. unsecured depositors; application of the “dominant legislation” doctrine; possible MCQ/short answer on whether Section 26E extends to MPID deposits and on the hierarchy between a central law (Entry 45, List I) and a state law in the context of recovery of dues.

title: Supreme Court Grants 3 Weeks' Interim Bail To AAP Leader Deepak Singla In Money Laundering Case
summary: A bench of CJI Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V Mohana passed the order after hearing Senior Advocates Vikas Singh and Balbir Singh (for Singla).

note.Facts: Deepak Singla, an AAP leader, was arrested by the Enforcement Directorate on 18 May 2026 in a money-laundering case linked to a Rs 155 crore bank fraud arising from a 2018 CBI complaint; he had been in custody for over six months and his father was ailing.
note.Issue: Whether the Supreme Court should grant interim bail to Singla pending the decision of the Punjab and Haryana High Court on his regular bail application.
note.Held: The Supreme Court granted interim bail for three weeks, subject to conditions and bail bonds, and directed the High Court to decide the pending bail application within that period.
note.Principle: The Court may grant interim bail without addressing the merits of the case when personal circumstances (e.g., ailing family member) and the protracted nature of the trial justify temporary release, while the lower court’s pending decision is left untouched.
note.Exam angle: Prevention of Money-Laundering Act (PMLA) – could be asked on the criteria for granting interim bail versus regular bail, focusing on personal hardship and trial delay as factors.

title: Supreme Court examines whether Corporate Debtor’s balance sheets constitute acknowledgement of debt under Section 18, Limitation Act in IBC proceedings
summary: Supreme Court: In an appeal questioning the dismissal of the Section 7 application filed by the appellant-Company under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (IBC) for being time-barred, the Division Bench of K.V. Viswanathan* and Arun Palli held that the balance sheets of the corporate debtor constituted clear acknowledgement of liability under Section 18 ,.

note.Facts: United Bank of India sanctioned a ₹12.26 cr loan to Kalpataru Cold Storage Ltd.; the first default occurred on 31 Dec 2013 and the account was declared NPA on 31 Mar 2014. The debtor’s balance sheets for FY 2015-16, 2016-17 and 2017-18 showed long-term borrowings and secured term loans. The appellant filed a Section 7 IBC application on 26 Oct 2018 claiming ₹21.61 cr, which the NCLT admitted on the basis of those balance sheets. The NCLAT reversed, holding the statements did not amount to acknowledgement of debt and the claim was time-barred.
note.Issue: Whether the Section 7 application filed on 26 Oct 2018 was within the limitation period, i.e., whether the debtor’s balance sheets constitute an acknowledgement of liability under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963.
note.Held: The Supreme Court held that the balance sheets for FY 2015-16, 2016-17 and 2017-18 clearly acknowledge the subsisting liability; consequently, the Section 7 application was filed within limitation. The NCLAT’s judgment was set aside and the matter remitted to the NCLT to decide only the question of default under Section 7(5) IBC.
note.Principle: An entry in a corporate debtor’s balance sheet that records long-term borrowings or secured term loans, together with surrounding disclosures, can constitute an acknowledgement of liability under Section 18, Limitation Act, 1963; the provision must not be applied with “pedantic rigidity” in IBC proceedings.
note.Provisions: Section 7, IBC, 2016; Section 18, Limitation Act, 1963; Section 13(2), Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002; cases: *Dena Bank v. C. Shivakumar Reddy* (2021) 10 SCC 330, *Vidyasagar Prasad v. UCO Bank* (2024) 251 Comp Cas 636, *IL & FS Financial Services Ltd. v. Adhunik Meghalaya Steels (P) Ltd.* (2026) 3 SCC 794.
note.Exam angle: IBC – limitation of a Section 7 petition; focus on “acknowledgement of debt” under Section 18, Limitation Act. Could be asked to frame the issue of whether financial statements qualify as acknowledgment, or to list the ingredients (written acknowledgment, reference to liability, contemporaneity) required for invoking Section 18 in IBC cases.

title: Supreme Court: Judicial member mandatory for final adjudication under PMLA; single non-judicial member can issue show-cause notice
summary: Supreme Court: While examining the validity of the Constitution and functioning of the adjudicating authority (AA) under the Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002 (PMLA), a three-Judge Bench of Surya Kant, CJ with Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana, JJ. , held that the Bench undertaking final adjudication under Section 8(2) and (3) PMLA must necessarily include.

note.Facts: The Adjudicating Authority (AA) under the PMLA issued a show-cause notice under Section 8(1) through a single Technical Member (non-judicial) who was also the Chairperson; the validity of such a single-member, non-judicial bench and the requirement of a Judicial Member for final adjudication were challenged before the Supreme Court.
note.Issue: Whether a Bench of the AA that decides matters under Section 8(2)-(3) (final adjudication) must include a Judicial Member, and whether a single non-judicial Member can issue a show-cause notice under Section 8(1).
note.Held: The Court held that any Bench undertaking final adjudication under Section 8(2)-(3) must necessarily include a Judicial Member. However, the issuance of a show-cause notice under Section 8(1) may be made by a single Member, even if that Member is non-judicial. The Chairperson need not be a Judicial Member.
note.Principle: Final adjudicatory decisions under Section 8(2)-(3) of the PMLA require the presence of a Judicial Member on the Bench; a single-Member bench (including a non-judicial Member) may validly issue a show-cause notice under Section 8(1).
note.Provisions: Sekar v. Union of India (2018 SCC OnLine Del 6523); R.P. Infosystems Ltd. v. Adjudication Authority PMLA (2023 2 HCC (Cal) 251).
note.Exam angle: PMLA – composition of the Adjudicating Authority; focus on Section 8 (show-cause notice vs. final adjudication) and Section 6 (bench composition). Questions may ask to frame the issue of “mandatory judicial member for final adjudication” or to list the ingredients for a valid bench under the Act.

title: Stringent Bail Conditions Under NDPS Act Can't Displace Special Protection Afforded To Juveniles: MP High Court
case_name: Child In Conflict With Law v. State of MP
summary: Madhya Pradesh High Court judgment in Child In Conflict With Law v. State of MP.

note.Facts: The bench considered a petition for bail where the accused, a juvenile, was charged under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act and the Juvenile Justice (JJ) Act.
note.Issue: Whether the stringent bail conditions prescribed under the NDPS Act can override the child-specific bail framework under Section 12 of the JJ Act.
note.Held: The High Court held that the special protection afforded to juveniles under Section 12 of the JJ Act prevails; bail is the rule for juveniles and denial is the exception, regardless of NDPS-Act conditions.
note.Principle: When a statute provides a special, child-specific bail regime, that regime cannot be displaced by the general, stricter bail conditions of another law.
note.Provisions: Section 12, Juvenile Justice Act; NDPS Act (bail provisions – not specified). No other cases cited.
note.Exam angle: Conflict between the NDPS Act and the Juvenile Justice Act – could be asked on the hierarchy of statutes and the rule that child-specific provisions under the JJ Act supersede other bail restrictions.

title: Strong Suspicion Of Conspiracy Sufficient To Deny Discharge Even In Absence Of Direct Evidence: Kerala High Court
case_name: P.M. Rajan v. State of Kerala
summary: Kerala High Court judgment in P.M. Rajan v. State of Kerala.

note.Facts: The second accused in a corruption case filed a discharge plea, which was rejected; the matter came before Justice A. Badharudeen on a revision petition.
note.Issue: Whether a mere strong suspicion of participation in a conspiracy, without direct evidence, is sufficient to deny discharge and proceed to trial.
note.Held: The court held that strong suspicion of involvement in a conspiracy is enough to justify a trial, even if direct evidence of the conspiracy is lacking.
note.Principle: A conviction can be pursued on the basis of strong suspicion of conspiracy; the absence of direct proof does not bar trial.
note.Exam angle: Could be asked under the Prevention of Corruption Act – focusing on the requirement of suspicion versus direct evidence to deny discharge.
